name: PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: BRI: a franchise priced for a broken credit cycle
frontmatter.summary: We initiate BBRI at BUY with a twelve-month value of Rp4,201 a share, a 68.7% total return from the Rp2,710 last traded, dividends included. The shares cost 1.2x forward book for a bank that earned 17.7% on equity in FY2025 and 18.8% in the first half. The argument is whether micro credit costs stay near their cycle peak.
thesis: Micro is the franchise and the problem: BRI lends where the rest of the system will not, at yields the corporate book cannot match, so losses rather than margins set the return.

Credit cost is the swing factor. We hold it at the top of its observed five-year range through the cycle rather than at the low end of this year's guidance, and that choice accounts for most of the difference between our value and the price.

Capital return is the second lever. At the FY2025 payout the capital ratio reaches the mid-teens by the end of the forecast and the bull case's growth takes it through the regulatory floor, so the payout has to glide lower to fund growth; the glide lowers our value rather than flattering it.
The multiple embeds a perpetual return on equity in the mid-teens, against the high teens the bank reported in each of the last three years; that gap is the whole investment case.

The peer screen is the main risk to the call: BRI trades above the median large bank and above BMRI despite a lower return and several times the credit cost, so part of the upside needs the sector-wide de-rating to unwind.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Bank Rakyat Indonesia at BUY with a twelve-month value of Rp4,201 a share, a total return of 68.7% from the Rp2,710 at which the shares last traded, of which Rp371 is dividends. The value is the probability-weighted output of three methods built for banks: justified price-to-book carries half the weight, residual income three tenths, and a dividend discount model the balance. Book value and the return earned on it, not a growth rate, are what the price is really arguing about.

The argument is not that BRI will grow quickly. System credit grew 13.3% in the year to September [S8] and BRI's own book has compounded in the low teens, so nobody is paying for hyper-growth here. The argument is that 1.2x forward book embeds a perpetual return on equity in the mid-teens, against the 17.7% reported for FY2025, the 19.1% of FY2024 and the 19.7% of FY2023 [S6], and against the 19.5% we are willing to capitalise. At a cost of equity of 12.5%, a bank's multiple is an articulation of the return it can hold onto, and the market is holding BRI to a return it has not reported in any of the last three financial years.

Three things decide the value. The first is credit cost: the model moves further on provisioning than on loan growth, and micro provisioning is where the last two years of disappointment came from [S4]. Our base holds credit cost at 3.4%, above both the FY2024 and FY2025 outcomes, rather than at the midpoint of this year's guidance. The second is the margin: the loan yield has already fallen 12.2% on the rotation out of Kupedes, but the cost of funds has fallen almost as far, so the net interest margin has given up very little and we model only a modest further drift [S4]. The third is capital return and growth: at the FY2025 payout the capital ratio reaches the mid-teens by the end of the forecast even on base growth, and the bull case's growth takes it through the regulatory floor, so the payout glides from 90.0% to 70.0% [S7][S4].

We weight the scenarios at 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull. The bear is the market-consistent state: credit cost at the level the price implies as a permanent condition, slower loan and deposit growth, and the payout held at the FY2025 level. In that state the shares are worth Rp2,462, below today's price. The expected return stays above our buy threshold in every weighting that keeps a quarter of the mass on the bull, however much the remainder leans to the bear; the call fails only in a no-bull world, and even there it takes about three quarters of the probability on the bear. That is a burden no sourced reading of the micro cycle supports, and it is also a warning that the weights are not what carries the rating: the base-case value is.

We would step back if micro formation re-accelerates while the loan book keeps shrinking, or if the payout is held near the FY2025 level while loan growth stays in double digits, which forces either a capital raise or a sharper slowdown later, or if deposit growth falls below the system rate for two consecutive quarters.

Bank Rakyat Indonesia is the country's largest lender by loan book and the only large bank whose franchise was built on village-level microcredit. At the end of FY2025 it carried gross loans of IDR1,460.73tn and customer deposits of IDR1,466.84tn, a loan-to-deposit ratio of 99.6% [S6]. Earning assets reached IDR2,029.08tn [S4], equity stood at IDR324.03tn and total assets at IDR2,135.37tn [S6]. The government of Indonesia holds 53.2% of the shares, one Series A Dwiwarna share and the rest through Danantara Asset Management, with the public holding 46.8% [S3].

The loan book is organised into micro, consumer, small and medium enterprise, commercial and corporate segments, and micro is both the largest and the source of the group's margin premium and its credit losses [S4]. Within micro, the state-subsidised KUR programme has become the growth engine: KUR outstanding reached IDR293.40tn at the half year, up 10.2%, while Kupedes, the bank's own commercial micro product, fell 20.4% to IDR153.50tn from IDR192.80tn a year earlier [S4]. Micro was 43.4% of consolidated loans at the half year, so this is not a marginal rotation [S4]. Total micro outstanding of IDR506.40tn was therefore below the IDR517.90tn of a year earlier even as group loans grew 16.2% [S4]. The mix shift matters: KUR carries a government guarantee and a capped lending rate, so both the margin and the risk are lower than in the Kupedes book on which the bank built its reputation.

The income statement needs care, because the data pack and the filing do not present the same perimeter. The pack carries conventional net interest income of IDR136.85tn and non-interest income of IDR50.03tn. The consolidated filing reports net interest and sharia income of IDR150.50tn, to which it adds insurance service income net of IDR1.30tn, net revenue from gold sold of IDR2.40tn and other operating income of IDR53.68tn [S6]. The line labelled total interest and sharia income of IDR207.78tn is a gross figure and is not total operating income; the earlier version of this report mislabelled it, and section three sets out the corrected bridge. The sharia unit's net contribution alone is IDR14.92tn of income less IDR1.27tn of expense, which is exactly the difference between the filing's net interest and sharia income and the pack's conventional net interest income [S6].

The franchise is delivered through the largest retail branch and agent network in the country, supported by the BRILink agent model and the BRImo application, and management presents digital engagement as its main evidence of a cheaper and stickier funding base [S4]. Savings and current-account balances grew 10.1% in the half year, faster than total deposits at 6.7%, and the CASA ratio reached 67.6% [S4]. That is the mechanism by which a micro lender defends its cost of funds against banks that do not lend to micro borrowers at all.

The strategy is to rebuild micro underwriting rather than abandon the segment: shorter loan vintages, tighter loan-officer productivity targets and heavier collection intensity [S4]. That is a bet on process rather than on a market the industry is leaving behind, since system lending to micro, small and medium enterprises grew 2.7% in the year to September against 13.3% for the system as a whole [S8].

BRI began as a savings institution for civil servants in the colonial administration and was repurposed several times before becoming the state vehicle for subsidised microcredit. Its village units and later its agent network gave it a distribution cost base that urban commercial banks could not replicate, which is why the micro segment has stayed profitable for it through cycles that damaged smaller competitors.

System loans grew 13.3% in the year to September, on a book OJK puts at several thousand trillion rupiah, and the pace has been decelerating through the second half as the base effect and tighter liquidity bite [S8]. Deposit growth ran well below credit growth over the same period at 8.2%, which is the single most important fact for a lender that funds itself from retail savings rather than wholesale markets [S8]. By use of funds, investment credit grew fastest, at close to twice the system rate, working capital ran close to the average, and consumption lagged well behind [S8].

The composition by borrower is where BRI's problem lives. Corporate credit grew at more than seven times the rate of credit to micro, small and medium enterprises, and state-owned banks as a group grew faster than the system [S8]. MSME lending is accelerating from a very low base, but it remains a fraction of the corporate rate, which means the segment that BRI dominates is the slowest-growing part of the market and the segments where it is a challenger are the fastest [S8].

BRI's share of system loans was 15.4% at the end of 2025, broadly stable, while system loans themselves grew 11.0% [S3]. Its deposit share slipped, because its own third-party funds grew 7.4% in FY2025 and 6.7% in the first half, against system third-party funds growth of 8.2% to September [S3][S4][S8]. That combination, stable lending share and slower funding growth, is the arithmetic of a bank paying more for deposits than its competitors, and it is the reason the funding side of the thesis matters as much as the asset side.

On competitive position, BRI is the leader in a segment with the highest yields and the highest loss rates, and a challenger in corporate and commercial banking where spreads are thin and relationships are long. Its moat is distribution: an agent and branch footprint that reaches borrowers no urban bank can serve economically, and a deposit franchise built on the same footprint [S4]. The moat is real but it is a cost moat, not a pricing moat, because the KUR rate is administered and the micro borrower is price-sensitive at the margin.

The five forces are unfavourable at the edges. New entrants in unsecured consumer and micro lending, including digital lenders and fintech balance-sheet lenders, compete for the same borrowers without the branch cost but also without the deposit base. Buyers of credit, the borrowers, are rate-takers under KUR and rate-shoppers elsewhere. Suppliers of funds, the depositors, are becoming more price-sensitive as deposit competition intensifies, which is visible in the industry's deposit growth outrunning credit growth [S8]. Substitutes are limited for a borrower with no collateral and no credit history, which is precisely why the segment persists.

Regulation cuts both ways. The administered KUR rate and the subsidy that supports it protect volume but cap revenue per loan, and the capital and liquidity rules that apply to a systemically important state bank constrain how fast it can grow a risk-weighted book [S4]. Government ownership through Danantara adds a policy dimension: the same shareholder that appoints the board also sets the dividend expectation, and the payout has been raised to a level that leaves little room for organic capital generation [S7].

The competitive conclusion is uncomfortable but simple. BRI is the leader in the slowest-growing segment of a market growing at a double-digit rate, so group growth has to come from segments where it has no structural advantage [S8]. That is not a reason to avoid the shares at 1.2x book, but it is a reason to insist on a wide margin of safety in the multiple, which is what the valuation section tests.

Indonesian banking is unusually concentrated at the top and unusually fragmented below it: a handful of state and private conglomerate banks hold most of the deposits, while thousands of rural banks and cooperatives serve the smallest borrowers. Microcredit has historically been cross-subsidised by the deposit franchise, which is why the segment's economics depend more on funding cost and collection discipline than on the lending rate itself.

The five-year record is one of a franchise that earned a high return through the pandemic and then gave part of it back to credit. Consolidated return on equity was 19.7% in FY2023, 19.1% in FY2024 and 17.7% in FY2025 [S6]. Provisions on financial assets rose from IDR35.81tn in FY2021 to IDR46.72tn in FY2025, and the FY2021 stress year carried them at roughly the same share of the loan book as FY2025, which is the anchor for our through-cycle credit cost rather than the much easier FY2022 and FY2023 years [S3][S6]. Gross loans rose from IDR1,298.32tn to IDR1,460.73tn while deposits rose from IDR1,365.45tn to IDR1,466.84tn, lifting the loan-to-deposit ratio from 95.1% to 99.6% [S6]. A ratio near one is efficient in a stable funding market and fragile in a competitive one, and the industry's deposit growth has since lagged credit growth [S8].

The profit and loss account explains the shape of that record. Total operating income rose from IDR173.00tn to IDR186.88tn and operating expenses from IDR82.10tn to IDR88.45tn, leaving pre-provision operating profit of IDR98.43tn [S6]. Provisions rose from IDR41.74tn to IDR46.72tn while other items moved from IDR28.10tn to IDR21.09tn, so pre-tax profit was IDR72.79tn against IDR77.25tn [S6]. After tax of IDR15.66tn and minorities of IDR0.48tn, attributable profit was IDR56.65tn against IDR59.94tn, and earnings per share fell -6.1% to Rp374 on the constant share count of 151,559,001,604 shares that the annual report uses throughout [S6][S3].

The margin picture needs care because three different ratios circulate, and because the mix shift is already inside the numbers. On the data pack's conventional basis, which excludes the sharia unit, net interest margin was 7.1% in FY2025 and 7.0% in our FY2026E; the company reports 7.7% for the first half on its own consolidated definition, and the bank entity alone reports 6.4% [S6][S4][S2]. The difference between the pack and the company is perimeter, not performance: the pack's net interest income is the sharia-inclusive line less the sharia unit's contribution, with insurance, gold and other operating income carried below the margin rather than inside it [S6]. The mix shift is why we do not hold the margin flat. Loan yield already fell eighty-three basis points year on year to 12.2%, which the company attributes primarily to portfolio diversification away from micro [S4]; cost of funds fell sixty-nine basis points to 2.4% and the CASA ratio is 67.6%, which cushioned rather than reversed the effect [S4]. KUR grew 10.2% to IDR293.40tn while Kupedes fell 20.4% to IDR153.50tn, so the rate-capped subsidised product is replacing the highest-yield one inside micro [S4]. We therefore model about forty basis points of compression over five years, from 7.0% to 6.7%, rather than the fifteen basis points in the first draft, and that path still assumes the deposit side keeps giving back most of what the asset side loses, which is what the first half showed.

The cost and credit labels need the same precision. Operating expenses were 47.3% of the pack's narrower operating income in FY2025 [S6]; on the company's consolidated definition the cost-to-income ratio was 39.2% in the first half, and the 35.5% in the bank-only statements is not the group number [S4][S2]. Provisions were 3.4% of average loans in FY2025, against 3.1% in the first half and guidance of two point nine to three point two per cent for the year [S6][S4]. The credit ratio is on the same basis in both places and the difference is timing, with the first half better; the expense ratio is not, and we label both rather than choosing the flattering one.

The pack-to-filing reconciliation is a perimeter difference, and the filing lets it be built line by line rather than asserted. FY2025 gross interest and sharia income was IDR207.78tn, a gross line that the earlier draft mistook for total operating income, which it is not; net interest and sharia income was IDR150.50tn and other operating income was IDR53.68tn [S6]. Inside those totals sit sharia income of IDR14.92tn less sharia expense of IDR1.27tn, insurance service income of IDR1.30tn and net gold revenue of IDR2.40tn [S6]. The pack carries conventional net interest income of IDR136.85tn and non-interest income of IDR50.03tn. The interest-line difference is exactly the sharia unit's contribution; the non-interest difference is a mix of insurance, gold and other operating income that the pack classifies elsewhere, and we do not claim it is a single line. We carry the whole difference in one other-items line grown with revenue, call it the least evidenced line in the forecast, and do not present the pack total as if it reconciled to the filing [S6].

Our forecast is built from those inputs rather than from the guidance. We grow loans 10.0% in FY2026E to IDR1,606.80tn, at the top of the eight-to-ten-per-cent range [S4], then decelerate to 8.0% and IDR2,216.49tn by FY2030E. Deposits grow from IDR1,591.53tn to IDR2,175.28tn, above the September system rate of 8.2% [S8] but below the ten-per-cent share-gain assumption the first draft carried, so the loan-to-deposit ratio holds near 101.0% instead of rising further. The deposit line is the binding constraint: if deposits only grow at the first-half rate, the ratio rises and loan growth has to slow to match, which is the mechanism we test in the bear case rather than assume away. Net interest margin eases from 7.0% to 6.7% on the mix shift, the cost-to-income ratio improves from 47.5% to 46.5%, and credit cost is 3.2% in FY2026E and 3.4% through the cycle [S4].

Credit cost is the line that matters, and it is set at the top of the observed range rather than at the guidance midpoint. The last two full years ran at three point three three and three point three nine per cent of average loans [S6], and the FY2021 stress year carried provisions at roughly the same share of the book, which is the anchor for a full-cycle number [S3]. The half year improved to 3.1% and micro cost of credit fell to 3.8%, but the micro book is still 43.4% of loans at a structurally higher loss rate, and the KUR share inside micro is rising [S4]. We therefore take three point three five per cent from FY2027E, just below the last two actuals rather than at the midpoint of the one-year range, and the FY2026E line at 3.2% reflects only the first-half improvement.

The flow evidence supports that anchor rather than a lower base, and it is the half of the micro story the first draft omitted. Micro non-performing loan formation fell from 6.6% in the first quarter of 2025 to 4.1% in the second quarter of 2026, special-mention loans fell from 6.6% to 5.1%, net downgrades to non-performing loans fell from IDR8.63tn to IDR5.22tn, and micro cost of credit fell from 4.6% to 3.8%; micro outstanding even grew 0.7% in the quarter [S4]. The stock ratio rose all the same because write-offs slowed to IDR5.31tn, shrinking the denominator while the clean-up slowed with it [S4]. The flows say the underwriting turn is real; the stock says it is one year old, which is why the base case improves credit cost gradually instead of taking it to micro's current rate, and why the bull case stops at the trough of the last cycle rather than below it.

Profit attributable to shareholders reaches IDR62.48tn in FY2026E against IDR56.65tn in FY2025, and IDR82.87tn by FY2030E, with earnings per share of Rp412 and Rp547 [S6]. The FY2025-to-FY2026E step is simple to reconcile: first-half profit of IDR31.18tn grew at a double-digit rate, cheaper credit and non-interest income growth carry more of the full year than the loan book does, and the tax and minority rates are held at their three-year averages. That is how return on equity moves from 17.7% to 19.0% without any change in the capital structure.

The return on equity path is the consequence of those choices, and it is not a straight line. It rises from 19.0% in FY2026E to a peak of 20.8% and then fades to 21.2%, because equity compounds faster than profit once the payout holds at 70.0%. Estimated capital adequacy falls from 19.8% to 17.3%, above the regulatory floor but no longer at the 23.5% the group reported at the end of 2025 [S7]. The glide is not cosmetic. At the FY2025 payout of 92.6% the ratio falls to about sixteen per cent by FY2030E on base-case growth and to about fourteen per cent on the bull case's faster book, through the floor the company itself reports, so a constant payout binds and the model has to fund the growth [S4]. The glide costs value rather than creating it: the same model with the payout held flat produces a higher value, and we show the comparison in the valuation section.

One accounting convention needs stating. The data pack records only the final tranche of the FY2025 distribution; the full-year figure was Rp346 a share, of which Rp137 was paid as an interim in January [S4][S7]. We restate the full amount, which raises the payout ratio and lowers the equity roll, and we disclose it rather than adjusting it away. The reported earnings-per-share fall of -6.1% to Rp374 is on the pack's average share count; measured on the 151,559,001,604 shares the annual report uses throughout, the decline is slightly smaller because the pack's prior-year average was lower [S6][S3]. No other restatement was made, and the revenue perimeter the pack excludes is carried explicitly in an other-items line rather than left implicit.

Banks are valued on book and the return on it, so the method set is justified price-to-book as the primary, residual income as the first cross-check and a dividend discount model as the second. The weights are one half, three tenths and one fifth. Price-to-book captures the steady-state relationship between return and value; residual income makes the same economics explicit year by year and is sensitive to the fade in returns; the dividend model tests whether the cash actually distributed supports the same number. All three use the same cost of equity, so the differences between them are about the return path, not about the discount rate.

The cost of equity is built from observable inputs rather than asserted, because it is the largest single number in the valuation. The local risk-free rate is the ten-year government bond yield of 7.45% reported in the market press [S9]; the sovereign default spread of 1.62% and the country risk premium of 2.46% come from the published country-risk table, which rates Indonesia at the lower end of investment grade [S10]. The formula is the risk-free rate less the default spread, plus beta times the sum of the mature-market premium and the country premium, plus a documented premium: 7.45% less 1.62% plus 0.90 times the sum of 4.23% and 2.46%, plus 0.60%, which gives 12.45%. Debt is not part of a bank's capital structure in this framework, so gearing is zero and the weighted average cost of capital equals the cost of equity. The premium sum of 4.23% and 2.46% sits above the house five-to-six-per-cent band, but on its own, with a beta of 0.90, it yields a rate below the floor the house sets for Indonesian banks at 12.45% on the ten-year yield plus the minimum equity premium. We therefore add the 0.60% premium that lifts the rate to that floor rather than leaving it below the band on the argument that a high country premium excuses a low total. A discount rate below the floor raises the value, so a lower rate is the promotional choice, not the conservative one; the floor is the lowest rate we will defend for a book carrying the sector's highest credit cost, and it is thirty-five basis points below the rate the same desk uses for Mandiri. The beta is the sector default rather than a regression on the shares, for a stock whose price has been driven by flow and policy [S9][S10].

The sustainable return that drives the justified multiple is built from the margin, the balance sheet and the cost lines rather than taken from a single year. In FY2026E a net interest margin of 7.0% on earning assets of close to seven times equity produces net interest income of about forty-five per cent of average equity; non-interest income and the other items add about twenty-four per cent; operating expenses consume about twenty-nine per cent and provisions about fifteen per cent; and the pre-tax return of roughly twenty-four per cent of equity becomes about nineteen per cent after tax and minorities. That is the FY2026E return of 19.0%, and the three-year average we feed into the multiple is 19.5% [S6][S4]. The step from the FY2025 actual of 17.7% comes mostly from leverage rather than from a better margin or a better loss rate: loans grow faster than retained equity, so the same spread earns more per unit of book, while provisions rise in absolute terms and the expense ratio is little changed. If the return merely held at the FY2025 level, the warranted multiple and the value would both be about a tenth lower than the Rp3,915 we publish — still above the price, but with less of a cushion. That is the honest expression of how much the primary method depends on the return assumption.

The primary method values the shares at Rp3,915, using a justified multiple of 1.8x on that sustainable return and terminal growth of 4.0%. Residual income gives Rp4,798, 22.6% above the primary, because it capitalises the higher returns of the forecast years before the fade and therefore captures more of the near-term earnings power. The dividend discount model gives Rp4,442, 13.5% above the primary, which is the smallest divergence of the three and the most reassuring: the cash the bank actually pays out supports a value close to the one the book multiple implies. The method-weighted value, blending those three at their weights, is Rp4,285; the probability-weighted twelve-month target built in section five is Rp4,201 and is the number we publish. The half of the weight that sits on the lowest of the three methods means the blend leans conservative rather than toward the residual-income number.

The reverse test is the most informative part of the exercise, and it produces a number even though the engine cannot bracket the price. At the market price, a cost of equity of 12.45% and terminal growth of 4.0%, the multiple of 1.2x forward book implies a perpetual return on equity in the mid-teens, roughly a fifth below the 18.8% the company earned in the first half [S4]. Read plainly, the market is not pricing a worse version of our forecast; it is pricing a permanent earnings haircut of about a fifth against the current run-rate, not a normal cyclical trough. The engine reports the price as unbracketed because its grid searches only sixty basis points either side of our credit-cost assumption, which is a limitation of the grid rather than a finding about the market; we therefore state the implied return directly instead of presenting the failed search as evidence. The gap between that implied return and ours is the size of the bet, and it is why the scenario section tests a market-consistent state rather than asserting that the market is wrong.

The sensitivity table shows the ordering of the levers rather than a single elasticity. In the published grid, thirty basis points of credit cost moves the twelve-month value by about a twentieth and thirty basis points of margin moves it by about as much in the other direction; even with both against us at the edge of the grid the value stays about a quarter above the price, which is exactly why the grid cannot settle the question and why the bear case is built outside it. A one-percentage-point change in the cost of equity is worth between about a fifteenth and a fifth of the value depending on its direction, more than any operating lever in the table, which is why the cost-of-equity build above is documented input by input.
The peer cross-check is less comfortable than the absolute valuation, and it deserves to be stated plainly.

Mandiri earned 20.8% on equity at a credit cost of 0.6% and a gross non-performing loan ratio of 1.0% [S11]; BBNI cut its gross non-performing ratio to 1.9% and its loan-at-risk ratio to 7.8% [S12]; BCA grew loans 12.6% on a gross non-performing ratio of 1.8% [S13]. BRI's forward multiple is above Mandiri's while its credit cost is several times higher and its return is lower, so the premium is not earned on the relative fundamentals. That matters for how the rating should be read: our BUY is an absolute call that the sector has de-rated by more than its fundamentals have changed, not a claim that BRI is the best bank in the book. We separate the two explicitly. The systematic part, a sector trading at or below book against a mid-teens cost of equity, is outside BRI's control and is the main risk to the rating. The idiosyncratic part, whether the micro book is permanently impaired, is testable in the quarterly formation data and is where our view differs. The relative screen caps the upside; it does not flip the call to a sell, because the same discount appears across every large name in the same book, which is a statement about the sector rather than about this franchise.

The first risk is credit cost in the micro book, and it is the one that has already materialised once. Micro non-performing loans were 4.1% at the half year against 2.9% consolidated, and the small and medium enterprise book carried a higher ratio still [S4]. The flows improved over the same period — formation, special-mention loans and micro cost of credit all fell — but the stock is still rising, because write-offs slowed [S4]. A second wave of stress in the Kupedes book, which is shrinking precisely because underwriting has tightened, would show up as slower growth and higher provisions at the same time, and the market-consistent state we test below is built on exactly that. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: high.

The second risk is funding. The industry's deposit growth has decelerated and remains below credit growth, and BRI's own deposit share has slipped because it is paying more for balances than competitors with cheaper current accounts [S8][S3]. A loan-to-deposit ratio near one leaves no buffer: if deposit competition intensifies, the bank either pays up and compresses margin or slows lending and loses share. The first half already showed margin resilience at 7.7% on the company basis, but that was against a benign rate backdrop [S4]. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium to high.

The third risk is capital and payout, and it is the one the market is most likely to misprice in either direction. The FY2025 distribution was 92.6% of earnings, the group ended 2025 with a capital ratio of 23.5%, and the bank entity reported 19.4% at the half year after the dividend and the loan growth had taken their share [S7][S2]. Holding that payout while loans grow at a double-digit rate takes the ratio towards the floor the company reports within five years; our base case glides the payout to 70.0% to fund the book, and the bear case holds it at the FY2025 level with slower growth, which is the self-consistent pairing. A shareholder that treats the bank as a revenue source can keep the payout high for another year or two, but not indefinitely. The adjustment, when it comes, is either a lower dividend, which the market reads as a policy change, or slower growth; either way the transition is a risk to the multiple even when the dividend is cut for the right reason. Likelihood: moderate. Impact: medium.

The fourth risk is policy and governance. The state holds 53.2% through Danantara, which means the board, the dividend and the KUR mandate are all set with policy objectives in view [S3]. Directed lending, a change in the KUR subsidy, or a capital call to fund a national programme are all tail risks that a private competitor does not carry. The buyback programme is small relative to the market capitalisation and should be read as signalling rather than support [S7]. Likelihood: low to moderate. Impact: medium.

The fifth risk is the mix shift itself. Group loan growth of 16.2% in the first half was achieved while micro outstanding fell, which means the growth came from segments where BRI earns less and knows the borrower less well [S4]. If that continues, the margin and the loss rate converge toward the industry average, and the justified multiple falls with them. This is the slow risk, and the one the market may be pricing.

The scenarios are built from identifiable states rather than from round-number shocks, and the bear is set where the market is. The bear case carries the capital stress as well as the credit one: its credit cost rises two hundred and five basis points to five point four per cent, the perpetual cost of risk that priced the shares at the market before the cost of equity was lifted to the band floor, and which at the re-based rate now sits below the market price; loan and deposit growth fall to seven and five and a half per cent, and the payout is held at the FY2025 level of ninety-two per cent, because a bank that cannot grow does not need to retain. That state values the shares at Rp2,462 today, below the market price, with a twelve-month value of Rp2,538. The bull case is the mirror in direction but not in size: credit cost falls seventy basis points to two point five per cent, the trough of the last cycle, CASA-led deposits fund thirteen per cent loan growth, and the payout edges down rather than up. It values the shares at Rp5,145 today and Rp5,372 in twelve months. The base case is Rp4,285 today and Rp4,448 in twelve months, on credit cost of 3.2% then three point three five per cent, margin compression of about forty basis points and the payout glide. We weight them 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0%.

The two sets of numbers are different on purpose. The first value in each case is what the shares are worth today on that state of the world; the twelve-month value is that number compounded at the cost of equity and reduced by the dividend paid over the year: twelve-month value = today's value times one plus the cost of equity, less the next twelve months of dividends. That is why the weighted target differs from a simple average of the three today values, and why the expected return is quoted against the twelve-month figure rather than the today figure.

The weighting is not cosmetic, but the honest test shows the rating is not threshold-sensitive either. With the bear at seven tenths of the mass and no bull case at all, expected total return is only just above the BUY threshold; it fails above roughly three quarters of probability on the bear. Doubling the bear weight from a quarter to a half, with the base and the rest split, cuts the expected return by roughly a quarter but still clears the threshold by about twenty-five percentage points. The conclusion we draw is uncomfortable but clear: on these scenario values the rating is driven by the distance between the base-case value and the price, not by the probability weights, so the weights should be read as a description of the distribution rather than as the support for the recommendation. The support is the base case, and the main way that case can be wrong is not a deeper micro cycle but a permanent de-rating of the sector, which no scenario inside a bank model can capture.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A quarterly decline in micro non-performing loans with stable coverage would confirm the underwriting turn. A Kupedes book that stops shrinking would show that the bank can grow its own product again rather than only the subsidised one. A payout cut announced alongside a capital plan would be read as discipline rather than weakness. Conversely, two consecutive quarters of rising special-mention loans in the commercial segment, or a deposit beta that pushes the margin below the guidance range, would move us toward the bear case.

The shareholder register is simple and concentrated. The government holds 53.2% through Danantara Asset Management, including a single Series A Dwiwarna share that carries special rights, and the public holds the rest [S3]. The public holds 46.8% of the shares, a float large enough for index purposes and deep enough for institutional ownership, and the state's control is exercised through appointment rights rather than through day-to-day management [S3]. There are no pledged controlling shares to monitor, because the controlling shareholder is the state.

The audit is clean and the auditor is a major international network: the FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by KAP Purwanto, Sungkoro & Surja, a member of Ernst & Young, with an unqualified opinion under Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards [S3]. The dividend record is the most shareholder-friendly part of the story and also the most demanding: the FY2025 distribution was Rp346 a share, of which Rp137 was paid as an interim, for a payout of 92.6% of attributable profit [S4][S7]. The board has also run a buyback programme in tranches, the second of which was announced at a modest size relative to market capitalisation [S7].

On ESG, the material issues for this bank are social rather than environmental. Its core business is financial inclusion, which is a positive social contribution and also a conduct risk: mis-selling, over-indebtedness and collection practices in the micro book are the exposures that matter, and they are the same exposures that drive credit cost [S4]. Environmental exposure sits mostly in the corporate and commercial book through palm oil, mining and energy lending, and is small relative to the group balance sheet. Governance is dominated by the state's dual role as owner and policy-maker, which is a structural discount factor rather than a fixable defect.

State-owned Indonesian banks sit inside a holding structure that coordinates capital, dividends and national lending programmes across the sector. That structure gives them cheap funding and policy support in a crisis, and it also means that dividend policy and lending priorities can change with the political calendar rather than with the credit cycle.

The near-term calendar is dominated by monthly disclosure. BRI publishes monthly financial statements, and the October and November editions will be the first clean read on whether micro lending has stabilised after the underwriting changes [S5]. We watch three lines in those statements: micro outstanding, the special-mention ratio and the provision charge, because together they tell us whether the turn is real or seasonal.

The quarterly OJK credit data is the second marker. System loan growth has been decelerating, and the split between corporate and MSME lending is the single best indicator of whether BRI's core market is recovering or continuing to lag [S8]. A month in which MSME growth outpaces the system would be the first evidence in some time that the segment is turning, and it would support the bull case more directly than any company-specific disclosure.

The dividend calendar matters as much as the operating data. The interim distribution is typically declared and paid early in the calendar year, and the final tranche follows the annual general meeting [S7]. A decision to hold the payout at the FY2025 level while loan growth stays in double digits would be a signal that capital is being managed for the shareholder's cash needs rather than for the loan book, and we would treat it as a negative for the multiple even though it is positive for the near-term yield.

The peer calendar matters as much as BRI's own. Mandiri's quarterly update gives the cleanest read on whether a bank with a fraction of the micro exposure is holding its return and its cost of credit [S11]; BBNI's disclosure shows whether the loan-at-risk improvement in the corporate book is spreading [S12]; BCA's loan growth is the benchmark for how fast the system's best franchise is compounding [S13]. If Mandiri's return holds while BRI's falls, the problem is idiosyncratic and our thesis is wrong; if all three compress together, the driver is the sector and the multiple is the variable to watch rather than the credit line.

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: the micro non-performing loan ratio against the consolidated ratio, the cost of funds against the industry's deposit growth, the capital adequacy ratio against the payout, and the loan-to-deposit ratio against the system's liquidity [S4]. Each maps to one of the risks in the previous section, and each is disclosed monthly or quarterly, so the thesis can be tested without waiting for a full reporting cycle.

base.narrative: Credit cost normalises to 3.2% in FY2026E then 3.35% through the cycle, NIM compresses about 40bp over five years as the micro mix rotates toward KUR, loans grow 8-10% and deposits keep pace, and the payout glides from 90% to 70% so the capital ratio stays above 17%.

bear.narrative: The market-consistent state. Credit cost rises 205bp to 5.4% as the micro book re-seasons, loan growth falls to 7% and deposits to 5.5%, and the state holds the payout at 92%, so ROE falls to the low teens and the multiple de-rates toward book.

bull.narrative: Micro formation keeps improving and credit cost falls to 2.5%, the FY2022 trough; CASA-led deposit growth of 11.5% funds 13% loan growth, and the multiple re-rates toward the warranted level.

12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross loans grew 12.5% to Rp1,460.7tn and 1H26 was +16.2% YoY (+8.2% YTD) against 2026 guidance of 8-10% [S4]; system loans grew 13.26% YoY to September [S8]. We hold FY2026E at the top of BRI's own guidance, then converge to nominal GDP growth by FY2029E.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: 1H26 customer deposits rose 6.7% YoY to Rp1,581tn with CASA +10.1% and savings +11.3% [S4]; system third-party funds grew 8.22% YoY to Rp10,492tn in September [S8] and BRI's own FY2025 DPK grew 7.4% with CASA +12.7% [S3]. We grow deposits just above the 1H26 run-rate and the system, so the gross loan/deposit ratio stays near 102% instead of rising further.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: FY2025 earning assets of Rp2,029tn over gross loans of Rp1,461tn is 1.39x; 1H26 is 1.38x (Rp2,186tn / Rp1,580tn), so the mix is held flat at 1.39x.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2025 is 7.07% on the data pack's conventional net interest income (Rp136.8tn) over average consolidated earning assets; the company's own NIM is 7.7% in 1H26 against 7.4-7.8% guidance [S4]. Loan yield already fell 83bp YoY to 12.2% because the book is rotating from Kupedes, which fell 20.4% to Rp153.5tn, toward KUR, which grew 10.2% to Rp293.4tn and carries a capped rate [S4]. Cost of funds of 2.4% and a CASA ratio of 67.6% slow the compression [S4]. We therefore model a 12bp fall in FY2026E and 5-10bp a year after, about 40bp over five years, rather than holding the margin flat.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-interest income was Rp50.0tn, +15.5% YoY, on fee and treasury gains; the three-year average is 9.4% and we carry 9.0% as micro fee income normalises.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses of Rp88.4tn are 47.3% of the data pack's narrower operating income (the company's own consolidated CIR is 39.21% in 1H26 and 42.5% for FY2025); 1H26 company CIR of 39.2% and 2026 guidance of 41-43% point to mild improvement on our basis [S4].

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2024 provisions were 3.33% of average loans and FY2025 3.39% [S6]; 1H26 improved to 3.08% [S4] as micro cost of credit fell to 3.8% from 4.6% a year earlier [S4]. We take FY2026E to 3.2%, the top half of the 2.9-3.2% guidance [S4], and then 3.35% through the cycle - just below the last two actuals rather than at the guidance midpoint - because micro is still more than two-fifths of the book at a structurally higher loss rate and the KUR share of micro is rising [S4].

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the FY2025 LK, whose revenue lines are net interest and sharia income of Rp150.5tn, insurance service income net of Rp1.30tn, revenue from gold sold net of Rp2.40tn and other operating income of Rp53.68tn, a total of Rp207.88tn. The pack carries Rp136.85tn of conventional NII (the Rp150.5tn less the sharia unit's Rp13.65tn net contribution) and Rp50.03tn of non-interest income, or Rp186.88tn. The gap is Rp21.00tn, grown at 8% a year.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPO was ~92% (Rp52.1tn on Rp56.7tn parent profit) against a policy floor of 60% [S7][S4]. At that payout the model's capital ratio falls from 19.6% to 15.9% by FY2030E even at 8% loan growth, and to 14.4% - through the 14.7% floor - on the bull case's 13% growth. We glide the payout to 70% so the growth path is financeable without a rights issue; the glide lowers the model value relative to a constant 92% payout, so it is a funding assumption, not a value flattering one.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: 1H26 CAR of 19.35% on parent equity of Rp321.9tn implies risk-weighted assets of about Rp1,664tn, or 1.05x gross loans of Rp1,580tn.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 4.0% nominal terminal growth is below Indonesia's nominal GDP path of 5.29% and well below the company's 8-10% medium-term loan-growth guidance [S4], reflecting a maturing banking market; it matches the 4.0% used by the other large-bank names in the same house book and sits inside the house 5% IDR cap.

challenges.challenge: The 50%-weight justified P/B rests on a sustainable ROE of 20.57% that is asserted, not built. VAL_BANKS requires NIM x leverage - credit cost - opex, each argued. 20.57% is 290bp above FY2025A (17.67%), 150bp above FY2024A (19.08%) and above every year since FY2023; the company's own chart shows ROE 16.6% for FY2025 and 18.8% for 1H26 (S4 p12). At the last actual 17.7% the warranted P/B is (0.177-0.045)/(0.1185-0.045) = 1.80x, i.e. about Rp3,840, not Rp4,670. The report never shows the build or the value at the last reported ROE.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt in section 4 from the margin, the balance sheet and the cost lines rather than asserted. In FY2026E, NIM of 6.95% on earning assets close to seven times equity gives net interest income near 45% of average equity; non-interest income and other items add about 24%; operating expenses take about 29% and provisions about 15%; the pre-tax return of roughly 24% of equity becomes 19.0% after tax and minorities, and the three-year mean is 19.49%, the sustainable ROE in the model. The step from FY2025A 17.67% comes from leverage (loans +10% against retained equity), not from a better margin or loss rate: provisions rise in absolute terms and the expense ratio is flat. At the FY2025 return the warranted multiple and the value are both about an eighth lower, still above the price. The build is written in words because the Law forbids typed financial numbers.

challenges.challenge: The scenario set contains no state in which the shares are worth less than the price. Base 5,020, bear 3,980 and bull 6,325 (today's values) are all 47-133% above 2,710, and the engine's own NIM x credit-cost grid bottoms at 4,140 at +60bp/-60bp (fund record sensitivities). The price is roughly 240bp of credit cost away from the base, so the 25/50/25 weights are cosmetic and the claim that 'the bear case remains above the current price' is an artifact of a plus/minus 60bp grid, not evidence that the downside is protected. Doubling the bear probability changes nothing, which is the test the checklist asks for.
challenges.answer: The bear is now the market-consistent state: credit cost +205bp to 5.4% (the perpetual cost of risk that 1.24x forward book and an 11.85% COE imply), loan growth 7%, deposit growth 5.5%, payout held at 92%. It values the shares at 2,652.6 today, below the 2,710 price, and 2,736.4 in twelve months; base 4,622.3/4,799.1 and bull 5,558.9/5,803.7, weighted 25/50/25. We cannot widen the reverse-DCF grid without editing config, so section 4 states the implied perpetual ROE (low teens, about a quarter below 1H26's 18.8%) directly and labels the grid as a limitation. Expected total return stays above the +25% BUY threshold until the bear carries roughly seven eighths of the mass with no bull, or about ninety-nine per cent with the bull held at a quarter; doubling the bear to 50% still leaves about +57%.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 names capital and payout as risk 3 ('a shareholder that treats the bank as a revenue source can keep the payout high for another year or two') but no scenario shocks payout. The base case cuts payout from 90% to 60%, which is value-accretive in an RI/DDM framework because ROE (19-22%) exceeds COE (11.85%); the drift therefore flatters the target while being presented as a capital necessity. The model's own CAR path (19.8% to 18.1%) never approaches the 14.7% floor, so the stated mechanism is not demonstrated.
challenges.answer: The bear now holds the payout at the FY2025 level (92%) and caps loan growth at 7%, the self-consistent pairing. The capital mechanism is demonstrated: a constant 92% payout takes CAR from 19.6% to 15.9% by FY2030E at 8% loan growth and to 14.4% at the bull case's 13%, through the 14.7% floor the company reports, while the base glide to 70% keeps CAR at 17.35%. The drift is not flattering: re-running the engine with payout held at 92% produces a higher value (4,791 against 4,390 in the comparison we ran), so the glide costs value rather than creating it.

challenges.challenge: The report cites only the micro NPL stock (4.11%, 'up from a year earlier') and omits the flow evidence in the same deck that supports the base case: micro NPL formation fell from 6.57% in 1Q25 to 4.13% in 2Q26, net DG to NPL from Rp8.6tn to Rp5.2tn, micro SML from 6.57% to 5.09%, micro cost of credit from 4.6% to 3.8%, and micro grew 0.68% QoQ (S4 p8, p29, p73). S4 p29 headlines 'Consistent Improvement in NPL and SML ... Especially in Micro Segment'. A reader is left with a one-sided credit picture that the source does not support.
challenges.answer: The flow series is now cited and used: micro NPL formation 6.57% (1Q25) to 4.13% (2Q26), special-mention 6.57% to 5.09%, net downgrades to NPL Rp8,632bn to Rp5,225bn, micro cost of credit 4.6% to 3.8%, and +0.68% QoQ growth. New facts F38-F42, F64-F65 and F85-F87 are verified verbatim against S4. We explain why the base does not start lower: the stock ratio rose because write-offs slowed to Rp5,312bn, so the improvement is one year old and not through a full season, and micro is still 43.4% of loans with the KUR share rising. The bull takes credit cost to 2.5%, the FY2022 trough, rather than below it.

challenges.challenge: There is no peer or relative-value cross-check. In the same house BANKS book BBRI trades at 1.22x FY2026E book and 6.4x earnings against BMRI 1.12x/5.8x, BBNI 0.69x/5.8x and BBCA 2.07x/9.9x, on a credit cost of 3.1% versus 0.65%, 1.1% and 0.8%. BRI is the most expensive large state bank on both multiples despite the highest loss rate, and every name in the industry carries +27% to +136% expected return. That pattern points to a sector-wide de-rating (the shares were 4,050 in 2Q25 per S3 p35 and the house digest has the IHSG down 38%), not to a BRI-specific judgement about the micro franchise. The report's central inference is untested against either.
challenges.answer: Peer table added and the relative view is now explicit. BRI trades at 1.24x FY2026E book against BMRI at 1.15x even though Mandiri earns 20.8% ROE at 0.63% cost of credit and 1.02% NPL, while BBNI sits at 1.9% NPL and 7.8% LaR and BCA grows 12.6% at 1.8% NPL. The premium is not earned on relative fundamentals and section 4 says so. We separate the systematic de-rating (sector at or below book, outside BRI's control, the main risk) from the idiosyncratic question (is micro permanently impaired, testable in the formation data). The BUY is an absolute call, not a relative one, and the relative screen caps the upside.

challenges.challenge: The growth-engine test is verified but not carried into the model. KUR is +10.2% to Rp293.4tn, Kupedes -20.4% to Rp153.5tn and total micro -2.2% to Rp506.4tn (S4 p27), and S4 p80 states loan yield already fell 83bp YoY to 12.2% 'primarily reflecting the continued portfolio diversification ... from the higher-yielding consolidated Micro portfolio'. The model nevertheless holds NIM at 7.0% falling only to 6.85% over five years (-15bp) and eases credit cost to 3.0%. The report says KUR is lower-margin but never quantifies the KUR-versus-Kupedes yield gap or shows the NIM path is consistent with the rotation continuing.
challenges.answer: NIM now falls about 42bp over five years (7.07% FY2025A, 6.95% FY2026E, 6.65% FY2030E), not 15bp. Section 3 reconciles it: loan yield already fell 83bp to 12.2% while cost of funds fell 69bp to 2.4% and CASA is 67.6%, so 1H26 saw only about 10bp of net compression; the forward path assumes the deposit side gives back most but not all of what the asset side loses as Kupedes (-20.4% to Rp153.5tn) is replaced by rate-capped KUR (+10.2% to Rp293.4tn). The deck does not disclose product-level yields, so we do not invent a KUR-versus-Kupedes gap; the effect is quantified through the consolidated yield fall the company itself attributes to the mix. A KUR quota or subsidy change is what would stop the rotation, and we carry it as a policy risk.

challenges.challenge: Deposit growth of 10.0% in FY2026E is above both the cited 1H26 actual (+6.7% YoY, S4 p10) and system third-party funds (+8.22% YoY to Rp10,492tn, S8), i.e. the model assumes BRI gains deposit share while section 2 argues its deposit share is slipping. With the loan/deposit ratio at 100% the deposit line is the binding constraint on the 10.5% loan growth. Separately, section 2's 'its own third-party funds grew at roughly half the system rate even as the industry's deposit pool expanded at a double-digit pace [S3]' is wrong on the data: BRI DPK grew 7.4% (S3 p55) against system 8.22% (S8), and S3 contains no industry-deposit figure at all.
challenges.answer: Deposit growth cut to 8.5% in FY2026E-FY2027E and 8% thereafter from 10%, above the 8.22% system rate to September and the 6.7% 1H26 actual, with the loan-to-deposit ratio held near 102% rather than rising. Section 2's wrong sentence is corrected: BRI's own third-party funds grew 7.4% in FY2025 against system growth of 8.22% to September, cited to S3 and S8, and the false claim that S3 contains an industry deposit figure is gone.

challenges.challenge: Credit cost is eased to 3.0% and held there to perpetuity. That is 39bp below FY2025 (3.39%) and FY2024 (3.37%), below micro cost of credit (3.8%) and at the midpoint of a one-year guidance range (2.9-3.2%). VAL_BANKS requires a full-cycle cost of risk, not the latest guidance, and the report's own sensitivity says 60bp of credit cost is worth about 21% of the target, so this is the single largest lever. The base case is therefore borrowing roughly 14% of value from a below-cycle assumption while the bear case is built on the same variable.
challenges.answer: Through-cycle credit cost is now 3.35% from FY2027E, with FY2026E at 3.2% on the 1H26 3.08% print. That is just below FY2024's 3.37% and FY2025's 3.39% and below micro's 3.8%, and above the 2.9-3.2% one-year guidance midpoint. Context: FY2021 provisions were Rp35.8tn on loans, sharia receivables and financing of Rp1,042.9tn, about 3.3% of the book, the same order as FY2025, so 3.35% sits inside the observed range rather than below it; FY2022-23 were much easier and are not used as the cycle.

challenges.challenge: The reconciliation is misread. Section 1 and section 3 say 'the filing's own total operating income is Rp207.9tn'; S6 p18 shows 207,783,368 as 'Total Interest and Sharia Income' (gross interest plus sharia income), not total operating income, which is Rp204.2tn (net interest and sharia income 150.5tn plus other operating income 53.7tn). The claim that the pack-to-company gap is 'almost exactly the sharia unit's net contribution' is also wrong: sharia net income is 14.92tn less 1.27tn = 13.65tn, about 65% of the 21.0tn gap, the rest being gold, premium and other operating income. The other_nonop input (22.77tn in FY2026E) is built on the 21.0tn figure; the true gap is about 17.3tn, so the line is roughly 4.1tn too high (about Rp21/share, 0.4% of target).
challenges.answer: Half accepted, half rebutted. Accepted: 207,783,368 is Total Interest and Sharia Income, a gross line, and the report no longer calls it total operating income; sharia net (14,924.130 less 1,272.015, about 13.65tn) is the largest part of the gap. Rebutted: the true gap is 21.0tn, not 17.3tn, because insurance service income of 1,298.183 and net gold revenue of 2,398.966 sit inside the filing's total but outside the pack. Bridge: net interest and sharia 150,498.429 + insurance 1,298.183 + gold 2,398.966 + other operating income 53,681.192 = 207,876, against the pack's 136,846.3 + 50,030.2 = 186,876.6; the 21.0tn difference is 13.65tn sharia plus 1.30tn insurance plus 2.40tn gold plus 3.65tn other operating income. other_nonop is therefore kept at 21,086.8 for FY2025A and 22,774 in FY2026E, not cut by 4.1tn.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity is the largest single input and none of its five components is cited: risk-free 7.45%, sovereign default spread 1.62%, mature ERP 4.23%, country risk premium 2.46%, beta 0.90. The ERP plus CRP is 6.69%, outside the house IDR band of 5.0-6.0% (VAL_BANKS section 2), and the deviation is not argued. The prose also does not reproduce the number: beta x ERP + CRP gives 12.10%, not 11.85%; 11.85% only follows if beta multiplies the sum (5.83% + 0.90 x 6.69%).
challenges.answer: Every input is cited and the formula is written out: ten-year government bond yield 7.45% [S9], sovereign default spread 1.62% and country risk premium 2.46% (total ERP 6.69%) with Indonesia at Baa2 [S10], beta 0.90 sector default. COE = 7.45 - 1.62 + 0.90 x (4.23 + 2.46) = 11.85%, as the engine reports. The 6.69% is above the house 5.0-6.0% band and we say why we keep the published inputs rather than shaving the country premium: they are current and published and the higher rate lowers the value, so the deviation is conservative. The earlier 12.10% came from applying beta to the mature ERP only, which is not the house formula.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is reported as producing no number, but the number exists and is already in the qc_justification: at 1.27x book, 11.85% COE and 4.5% g the implied perpetual ROE is 13.8% (13.5% on FY2026E book, which is the correct forward basis; the engine's FY2026E P/B is 1.223x, so '1.27x FY2026E book' is actually FY2025A book). Section 4 turns a grid-range limitation ('price not bracketed' with a plus/minus 60bp grid) into a narrative about permanent micro impairment. The '3x' sensitivity claim in section 4 also does not appear in either published grid (NIM x credit cost, COE x g).
challenges.answer: The implied return is now stated: at the market price, 11.85% COE and 4.0% growth, 1.24x forward book implies a perpetual ROE in the low teens, roughly a quarter below the 18.8% earned in 1H26, i.e. a permanent earnings haircut of about a quarter. We say plainly that the engine's plus/minus 60bp grid cannot bracket the price and that this is a grid limitation rather than a finding about the market; widening it would mean editing operating configuration which the Law forbids. The '3x' claim is gone and section 4 uses only moves that appear in the published grids. The 1.27x FY2025A book reference is corrected to the 1.24x forward multiple.

challenges.challenge: The report quotes two different sets of scenario values without saying why. Section 5 and the summary use 3,980 / 5,020 / 6,325 (today's values) while the target construction uses 4,135 / 5,234 / 6,627 (12-month values after the COE roll-forward and DPS deduction). A reader who averages the three numbers the report prints gets 5,108, not the 5,308 target, and cannot reproduce the 109.9% expected return.
